result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_periphery()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get periphery nodes (nodes with maximum eccentricity). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L20261-L20298){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_periphery() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Periphery nodes are farthest from the graph's center. These nodes have the maximum eccentricity (longest shortest path to any other node). Returns empty list if graph is disconnected. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs in the periphery, empty if disconnected. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Characteristics: - opposite of center: peripheral vs central nodes - in trees: always leaf nodes - multiple nodes can have maximum eccentricity ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a path graph `1-2-3-4-5`, the two endpoints are farthest from the graph's center, so they form the periphery: ::: {#3ebb63f9 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(5) periphery_ids = graph.get_periphery() # Returns 2 (the two endpoints) len(periphery_ids) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: :::
